speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Okay.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Amazing. Thank you so much for joining me today.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Thank you.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Can you start by telling me your name and pronouns?

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Okay, so my name is Brian Tinoota. I'm a heterosexual, male, so it's he. He/ Him.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Amazing. And then, where are you located, right now? And if you're from somewhere… somewhere else, where is that as well?

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: So I'm originally from Chipinge, which is the eastern side of Zimbabwe, but now I'm currently located in Harare, in the capital city.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Amazing. And then, how do you identify? Like, this can be about race and ethnicity, but it doesn't exclusively have to be about that.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: I identify as Black… What I can… what can I say? I don't want to say revolutionary, because I'm into Black revolutionary movements a lot, you know, but I… I ask… so professionally, I support everything which is pro-Black, pro-Indigenous people. So, indigenous economies, Indigenous organizations, African organizations, so those are the… the one I identify with. So, I can say… I can say I'm just an African. That's the best… the best description. I'm an African. Proudly African, yeah.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Amazing, amazing. And I'm curious about that distinction. Like, you started by identifying as Black, you also identified as African. You did not identify as Zimbabwean.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Yeah. You see, I'm Zimbabwean, and if you are staying in these countries, you tend to see that the idea of a nation is something that was brought on us, and if you come from a minority group, like where I come from, you can see the effects of this so-called nation, that you might not, end up, like, identifying with the nation as such.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Because I am Ndau, personally, I'm Ndau from Chipinge, it's a minority group. Yes, it's in Zimbabwe, but Some of our brothers are in Mozambique. So it's a… it's a group of people that was divided between Mozambique and Zimbabwe. And when we are back home, we just can just roam around the borders. So, if I can identify as Zimbabwean, it's kind of lying to myself that...

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: I think the African continent can just be the bigger boundary for us, because if we can just use one boundary now, if I'm a Ndau from Zimbabwe, then there's another Ndau from Mozambique, and yeah, that's why I didn't say Zimbabwe as such.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Cool. And then I was wondering if you could tell me a little bit about your family, and, like, what family looks like for you.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Okay. So, my family... So, I'm a father, starting from me. I'm a father of two. Then, I was raised by a single mother. So, I don't have… I didn't have, this mother-father family when I grew up. So my family from my father's side is much of an extended family that, we visited sometimes. So my relationship with them is not as close as to my mother's, because I grew up on my mother's side. And on my mother's side, I think because here in Africa, we call, like, if you are related, especially, especially, like, the people you can, like, name, okay, that they are coming from the same, maybe, great-grandfather, great-grandmother, you tend to be closer. The family will tend to be saying, like, "okay, this is family," so…

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: From my mother's side, we… her sisters, my mother's sisters, my aunties, and her children has been, like, part of my bigger family, so I call them sisters and brothers. Not cousins, we don't have any. We do not have our cousins, yes. Brothers and sisters, yeah.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Nice. And are both of your parents Ndau?

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Yes, kinda like. So, my mother is, like, the original Ndau, but, my father come from this, northern part of the… It's called Chimanimani, the other district. They speak Ndau, they are Ndau people in Chimanimani. But they kinda identify as the… The Garwe, the Garwe, like, the crocodile people. Though we speak the same, and, like, we don't have, like, a demarcation on where the now people are ending, and where these people are starting.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: But our history, the history of our family: it's like, they were mixed with the Ndau people at some point. They were displaced by the... The Nguni, the Nguni people who came from South Africa during the Mfecane period, they ended up being in the eastern side of Zimbabwe, where they created a kingdom called the Gungunhana Kingdom, the Gaza Kingdom, or the Gungunhana Kingdom. So, part of my family were displaced, they were taken to Mozambique, then some of them, they went… they had to come back after some period of time. I don't know how many years, but that's what they say. The evidence say, yes.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Thank you. I love talking to you, because I feel like I'm always getting a history lesson. And so I'm curious about what your relationship is to ancestry, right? Like, you talked a little bit about family in that immediate, but what does ancestry feel like for you in the longer sense of history?

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Like… I think at the moment, it's an unfortunate circumstance that we, as most Africans, find ourselves in that: we might know our ancestry, for some people who are still practicing the indigenous practices, like the traditional practices in Africa, that we… when we, consult the ancestors, we… because we consult them, when we find ourselves in predicaments. So we ask for help, or we ask for directions. So when we consult them, we tend to, mention names of, like, so if I'm… if it's me, I'll start from me to my father, my father's father, then to my great-great, until to the person that we still know with our heads, like, we still remember, because we didn't write the names down as such. Something that you could… you were supposed to know by heart. And, as the generation grows we no longer… some people no longer know the last person who… until… because we say, to the last eldest one who will take to the… to the Almighty, to the gods. So…

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: So relationship with ancestry, me as a person now, it's sad to say that since we didn't have, like good documentation of our lineages. It was, like, more of an oral history. Then, coupled with colonialism that came in between, and which told us that we were not enough, our spiritual practices were not enough, and we were supposed to be Christians. Then we're doing what we were doing, our African practices, is paganism, so we have to move away from that type of practices. So, which means we were stopped… we were… we now stopped reciting, like, calling names of our ancestors. We no longer put importance in, naming the names that came before us. In fact, like, we have to erase all that type of information from our heads, so that we can become born again. We now can call Jesus Christ, Abraham, and all the terms… the other types of names that are not related to us. So it's really unfortunate, like, if you had to look at ancestry from that way, as a person who knows what… what has happened for… to us, because… I, myself, asking the elders that are around me, they might mention a couple of names, and they seem not to care, because some of them, they are Christians. The…

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: I know for a fact that there are other names that got forgotten in the mix, because it's not like, our culture was all good, like, no. It was not all good, the person who was revered, maybe, was the person who was powerful, maybe richer, most of the times it is the male that will be venerated, like, who'll be revered, like respected. So where… What about the women? Because there are other matriarchies that were important, that get forgotten in the mix. And most of the times when they get mentioned, they might be mentioned in a bad way. Like, okay, if a daughter is failing to get married, we say, she has a spirit from this great-great-auntie who died without a husband. Like, there is no veneration for the mother, and it's kinda… It kind of got lost with, the patriarchal approach of the Western civilization that came with us… that came to us. Yeah?

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: I think I talked too much on one question.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: No, not at all, not at all. That's why we're here, to hear your answers.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: I'm curious, you know, you talked about how you identify as not just Black, but as a Black revolutionary. And so I'm wondering if there are particular ideas, from Ndau culture that feel like they drive your work, you know? So ideas like Ubuntu or, like, FUBU that are, like these kind of cultural ideologies that then, you know, manifest in the world. Are there things from Ndau culture that feel, like, drive your work?

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Yeah, yeah. So, if we had to talk about, Ubuntu and how is… how it drives our, my work… So the thing is, when we are living here in Africa, now it's a thing that it has been labeled that Ubuntu, but it's the other way of describing it is, like, a way of being a human. Like, if you were to literally translate it, it's the way of being a human. So, if you are a human who is, like, responsible and just, like you need to know that what you feel is what the next person feels. So you are… I am because this person is, even the way we greet each other.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: So we say, hi. So, if you say, good morning, I am okay if you are okay, that's how we respond to each other. So, I'm not okay if you are not okay. So it kind of validates the next person that you approach. So whenever we deal with each… with any person, we acknowledge the human being in that person, that, "okay, I exist because this person exists." The same things that are my intentions, because sometimes we feel like...

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: So, to the bigger, to take it bigger: so sometimes we've… we find ourselves fighting, as human beings, because we want to put my intentions forward over the next person's intentions, so whatever they… they… they want. What about if we approach it, like, from this perspective of, like: we know that maybe we might have, like similar intentions. Maybe it's a way of articulating those intentions so that we can find a common ground to achieve whatever we want to achieve. Because at the end of the day, we all want to live. We want to survive, and we want… we are just breathing the same… the same oxygen.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: So, if we… if you start, like, acknowledging the person in this next… in the next person, knowing that the person just needs also food, clothes, and shelter, whatever I'm going to do is not going to deny this person food, clothes, and shelter, if I'm to give some examples. If… whatever I'm going to do is not going to step on this person so that I can go up. So yeah, that's how I approach, like, how… Because it's… it's a way of life, that we… how we live it, yes.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Yeah, and is there… are there any words, like, in Ndau, or like, concepts that, yeah, that are Ndau specifically?

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Yeah, yeah, so the thing that is now specific is... So if you come to Zimbabwe, if you're, like, even if you Google about the Ndau people, Chipinge, they tend to associate us with witchcraft, black magic and stuff. Which is something that I really like, you know because… it's not because of the black magic of it, it's because the Ndau people, they embrace their indigenous practices. They are not shy to say we have went to consult a witch doctor for our problems. If something happens in their family, the whole family is notified that, oh, tomorrow, everyone is going to, like, a group of people is going to the witch doctor, so to consult and stuff. No matter whether the witch doctor is authentic, or will tell something true, is another… another argument, there's another argument for that. But my point is, this like, the idea of embracing the African spirituality in the Ndau people is so prominent. The idea of, embracing Indigenous medicine, because, when I am home, if I get sick, for example, I, I chopped myself, I cut myself on my hand or something, I can just pluck a herb that I know I grew… I'm not a witch doctor, but I know that this herb can heal my wound. I can just squish it and just put it on the wound. After a couple of days, it, it heals. There are some other medicines that we think, and I've seen that they have not been taken to laboratories, but they work.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: And, I have... Sorry, let me give you an example of what happened in 2023. My daughter, she was sick, she was so sick, and we went to the doctors, went to the hospital. They say it's dehydration. They prescribed us, like, the oral rehydration solution. We spent 2 weeks giving her that, and she was getting worse. And, my father-in-law saw her and says, like, oh, "this is something that we call in our language chipande. Just, you know, it's easy, you know, you just need to go to, an elderly lady. They know in our culture that how to treat such type of, of a disease." And we went to the lady, she's not any witch doctor or whatever, she's just an elderly lady. It's just a… it's kind of something like a common disease for… for kids, according to the Ndau people. And it can be cured easily. So he put… she put, like, some herbs on her two fingers, then she scratched inside my daughter's mouth, and my daughter vomited like a lot of mucus-like saliva. To tell you that tomorrow, the next… the day after, she was fine, but she spent 2 weeks unhealed by the conventional type of medicine, but this one, just like one day, because... And, they were like, "okay, why didn't you just come? Because this is something that is commonly known in our… you are trying to be Western, like, you go to the hospitals and stuff." So, the idea of embracing, some of the indigenous concepts, like, identifying with the African concepts, something that drives me from the Ndau people, specifically.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: That's amazing, I'm so glad that your daughter is doing better.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: And then I'm curious about, you know, similar to how you just defined something that was specific to Ndau people. What does it mean to be Black to you?

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Let me say to Black, it means a lot of things.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: It means... So, from, like, a facial recon… how we look, our features, the melanin in us. But I'm not going to dwell on that.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: So, for me, it means: a group of people, that is, that has been resilient through a lot of, persecution and they're still fighting for survival, in fact. And, they happen to be, coming from Africa, to be specific.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: And we have different shades of Blacks. We have people who are lighter, who are darker, and… But we share the common… common kind of dilemma, common problem, common… share common… share the common history. Yes, that's the right way. Share the common history.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Starting from way back then, when we're still used to be, the center of the civilization. Yeah, we built a lot of cities. We led in terms of civilizing the world. Then they come for an invasion. We all suffered foreign invasion, starting way back then with the Arab invasion. Slavery came through, Arab slavery, enslaving Black people. Then the transatlantic slave trade came, enslaving Black people, and they thought, "oh, it's no longer, profitable." They need… they had to enslave us in Africa. That's colonialism. And we are still fighting to get out of it. That's what, Black means for me.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Yeah, so that type of group that worked through a lot, and they are still resilient, they are still trying to fight back and, find their way, they are standing in this world. Yeah, that's what it means for me.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Thank you for sharing.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: And if you had to describe like, foundational Black worldview. How would you describe that? Like, something that you think is central to the Black experience and how we view the world.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Oh… Something that is central. I think it's to reclaim what we lost through, like, this period of persecution and all the stuff that happened. The idea of, like...

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Sorry, just… can you repeat your question? I was thinking… I still remember the question, but…

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: No, no worries at all. I was asking you if you had to describe a Black worldview what would that be?

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Foundation. Okay, the foundation is that: Everything that… not because everything that came, like, for any foreign invention, like… any foreign civilization was bad to Africa, no. It wasn't bad. But, the center of point of view of, like, the African, like, the pan-Africanist that I am… thinking of is to…

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: To readdress the effects of… Starting from slavery, colonialism, colonialism which came with mental colonialism. So that's the basic… the basis of it. There is… we feel like the fight isn't over. We are still trying to decolonize the mind. Yes, we kinda now have this independence, like, physical independence, but our minds… yeah. So…

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Yeah. And then, you know, like you… you said, there are, like are so many different Black experiences, right? And so I'm curious about if you have a story that you feel really exemplifies your experience of being Black. Like, if you have an anecdote or a personal story.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: My experience… So, my experience, I think starting coming from a place which was colonized, which meaning that the lands that we were staying in, they were not ours. They were owned by the white farm owners who had big farms, where our parents were working on the farms. My mother's still working on the farm. And so, it's kind of like, we were staying there, you don't have anywhere, you don't own any place, you don't have any land, and land is the basis of power. So you are just landless. So if you are landless, don't have any power. The boss, the white person who has the land can just chase you, fire you at will. And you find yourself… Begging another white person on another farm for you to work.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Then, fast forward, there was this, a land resettlement that happened in Zimbabwe. Where all the, the political elites grabbed land. So, my mother like, personally, my mother still works on the company that she was working. That company was not taken because it was a big company, it was not like a small firm. It was… it was not taken by the… so she's working under this big, it's a multinational company.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Then, now you are faced with this problem that you need to find some way to live so as a Black person, you now need to find your place in a place that used to be your place. So, if you are connected to the political elite, you... It's easy for you to get land. If you are not, you need to get rich, you need to find somewhere to work, get rich so that you can buy land. And, because of, the mismanagement that happened during this land resettlement era, it destroyed the economy, so there is no employment to be heard of.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: So it pushed us to look outside of Zimbabwe. That's where there's another… another experience of being Black is coming. Now, let me just take you back to Zimbabwe before I leave, from Zimbabwe. So, when you are in Zimbabwe, when you are a Black person. Just, you are there to struggle, like everyone else. If you are to talk about, like races, different type of races, not like there are no white people in Zimbabwe. There are white people in Zimbabwe, but they are not part of us as Black people. They, they stay in the elite suburbs of the towns. They go to their own schools that we can't afford. They go to, like to shop to those nice shopping centers that we can't afford most of the times. So, you just see them. So, the relationship, like, racial relationships is, like them and us. So, and most of the times, they have… economically, they have the economic power than the rest of us. Thus, the experience of, like a person growing up in Zimbabwe seeing, like, understanding race and the difference between races, then…

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Because of hardships, economic hardships, you are pushed to look outside. As I said, at some point, I found myself going to study a social entrepreneurship program in Sweden. There I had to experience another form of being Black that I didn't, like, know, like, as a person who was staying in Zimbabwe. This, thing that... So, when you are coming from Africa, in Zimbabwe, to be specific and if you have, like, the black revolutionary mind that I had, you might tend to… To see things, as black and white, and not also… And you'll not be able to differentiate between people, human beings as human beings. Not human beings, it's just like, okay, this white, and they would think the same, or this Black, and they think the same. So I had to… when I was living in Sweden, I had to see the difference between human beings. I had to say, "oh, they are white, but they are just human," because we used not to see them when we were in Zimbabwe. You see, we will see them from afar. We were… we didn't make contact. So the idea of making contact, letting your voice, like, what you stand for, like, what it means be known to the next… to the next race. And them to also, for them, for those… some of the people who were open enough try to address the misconceptions that they also heard about Black people, because for some, I was the first closest Black person that they had.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: So, it was another whole thing, of, of being Black, and, it kinda… Elevated, not… yeah. It kind of elevated my confidence at some point, sometimes that, my… my race is not inferior. The, like, how it is, like… how it is shown in where I come from in Zimbabwe, that the whites is the boss, and they have owned every… everything nice, and… and I had to, like… now, when I was living in a predominant white society, I could see also that: okay, a white person can be a beggar, is begging in the street, can be homeless, and all that. So, poverty doesn't affect only one race. But in a systematic… systematic, like, designed racial society, that's where you see, like, poverty kind of favoring a certain type of race. But in real life, in, so anyone can be poor, anyone can be rich. Then the segregation come with it.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Again, when you say that, the laws that operate, sometimes they are kind of targeting Black people. Talking about the other day, we were going into a ferry, trying to get into the ferry. We were a group of, what, 40 students? 40: four-zero. Everyone was going through and flowed, like, multiple nationalities. They spend, with everyone, with each and every one, they will spend, like, less than a minute to scan the… their passport, and they'll go to the… in the ferry, in the ship. But with mine, with my passport, because I was the Black guy, they took more than 5 minutes, and they had to ask other people, like, their superiors, to come and see this passport. It's like, okay, some… until my peers had to intervene, like, "okay, why him? Why are you just targeting him, and because we are all students, and we just passed through without any predicament," and you would see, like, okay, it's, like, you… if you're a Black person, you kind of carry a certain burden that you walk around with.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Another example is, we were supposed to leave Europe going to… to U, the UK, then leave UK to go to some internships. You would see that I was the only person who was struggling to get a visa. To each, like, even who will find himself needing a visa to go to a certain place. And, even with, like, letters supporting that I'm part of this, educational group, like, my first visa to the UK was denied, because I didn't, attach, what do they call it? A flight ticket that I will leave at the UK, when I… when what we want to do in the UK finished, like. So, that was another… that… I had an experience of being Black that, I had, yeah,

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Then, professionally working, you know, when you are working, maybe it's economics, and we understand that. But you tend to say… to say that, if you are Black, and if you are in Zimbabwe, if you are in Africa: financially, they expect to give you a lower wage than the rest of the groups, most of the times. Yes, they kind of have some… some justification about that, that, okay, it's because if someone is living in the UK, the cost of living is expensive in the UK as compared to the person who is living in Zimbabwe, and blah blah, and all sorts of those things. But, as a person who also kind of question this type of economics that we find ourselves, especially as Africans and the Europeans. If you were to read just Walter Rodney's, "How Europe Underdeveloped Africa" that, why is it most of the times that they have the capital, but we don't have the capital? So if they continue paying each other a lot of money, and me getting less money, aren't we repeating the same predicament that, now we can see a person with a… not a rich person as such in America, can come to Cape Town and buy a land in Cape Town, are pushing the people in Cape Town to move away from Cape Town, because now they can't afford to live in Cape Town. Because the people with capital are moving in with the money, because they are being paid more, a lot.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: What about if we had, like, an, if the people in Cape Town were being paid equivalent to what the person in America is being paid? You know, the person in Cape Town was not going to be pushed out of Cape Town. Because they don't have the amount of money to buy the land in capital. Yeah. So that's the other part of being black that I've been struggling with. And, experiencing professionally. Yep. I'll stop it here.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: No, no worries. I'm also curious about, you know, when you… When you first said that you identify as Black, you said it with a kind of pride, you know? And so I'm wondering what are some of the… On the flip side, you know, a lot of the experiences that you expressed were ones of… of struggle and of being oppressed and persecuted, I'm wondering what things you feel like being Black adds to your life, you know?

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: As… as for adding, it's like… the first thing is resilience. If you had to look at our history, what we have been through, resilience is a lot. So, I'm the type of a person who can walk through struggle with a smile. Not because it's not… it's not that hard. It's hard, but we know that we can get sailed through, so it keeps the spirit, like, and the mind, like, focused, that type of resilience, on the advantage, so it's our advantage.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: The idea of, for me that I can still, if I want, I can still trace my genealogy, my ancestry. I can still identify with the land, I can still identify with the land, eat from the land, get everything from the land, and live simple without the pressure of the Western civilization. So, I'm a person who can exist between two worlds. Living off the, like, just on the land without a lot of amenities, and being able to adapt to this Western type of a civilization, it's an advantage.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Then the other advantage is that I still speak my mother language. If you are to look at, now as a person who has traveled, and worked with other Indigenous people from other societies, we tend to say that in Africa, we are still are fortunate that, some of us, we still hold our Indigenous languages. We haven't forgot them. And now, at the moment, we are trying to include them in our educational curriculum so that we can… they can still remain. It's an… is an advantage. I don't think it must be an advantage as such, like, but something that I'm proud of. Because, if you are to look at the English, it's just a tribe of people who are speaking English. If we look at the Dutch, the German, the same thing, but it's not, like it's not, like, kind of officially recognized. If you are to come to Africa, that the Kikuyu people or the other people, like they are not being… serious nations, but it's, like, little tribes and stuff. But we are proud of that.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: The other thing that I'm on the advantage side, Oh. Yeah, I don't need to wear sunscreen. Yes, I need to say it here, because of my melanin, I don't need to wear sunscreen, yes. I just wanted to say it as a joke. Like, yeah, sometimes it's funny with my friends when we travel, like, okay, they need sunscreen, and I was like, oh, boy, I don't need it. I don't need this. I don't need this, yeah.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: What else? I'm being, yeah, I think those are from my head now, at the moment. Because sometimes, like, when life is so hard, sometimes we tend to know a lot of the negative things, but…

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Oh, the other thing. Yes, I know. The importance of family. In, like, family as, the… The basis of the society. Like, it starts with family, then we grow. So, like, it's… it seems like, in our communities, we have, like, a sense of community. Yes, strong sense of community. So, it starts from the family, then the immediate group, like, the village, and if you see someone from your village when you are away, they are, like, a member of your family. And if you see someone from your district when you are away, like, if you are seeing an Ndau person here like, so the sense of family, and… it's easier to adopt like among Black people, because I feel like, wherever I go, when I meet another Black person, even if they are from Nigeria, they will treat me like a brother. There is a certain type of understanding that we have.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: I still remember when I went to New York, at Ford Foundation, I was sitting with this lady from, I think it's Brooklyn. And, like, all of a sudden, we were just chatting, like, endlessly. We were talking about being Black, being African, and a lot of, like, what connects us, and the history that divided, us, that other people are finding themselves in the Western Hemisphere, and you could see her expressing herself, and she was so appreciative that she had to speak with a person from the motherland, from Africa, and I felt the same. I felt like I met a sister, and I was like, wow! So that sense of family… I don't… I can't explain it, I don't know if white people feel the same, but I feel it. Most of the times when I meet another Black person, it's not like everyone is the same, that, okay, when you meet someone, everything is kumbaya as such, but that's identifying with each other, yeah. It's great.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Totally. And then I have a… I want to start talking about your work experience, but before that, I have one last question, like, kind of on this, in the same light. Can you explain or describe to me the concept of Chimurenga.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Okay, the concept of Chimurenga is an uprising. So, the concept of a Chimurenga it was uprising against the white domination, white encroachment, white… the colonial system. So, there were two Chimurangas.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: The first Chimurenga was, in the early stages of colonialism when they completed the colonial project. After they completed the colonial project in 1890, so… So, here is how it happened. These people, they didn't come… like, the way they went in other areas, like in the Americas, when Columbus came to the Americas and stuff, they don't come guns blazing. They come with, like, they want to talk to the leaders, they sign some concessions, and without you knowing, you'll find yourself, like, under their authoritarian rule, their colonial rule. So, the Black people in Zimbabwe were under that colonial rule by 1890. And the leaders… the Black people that were there back then, they started to see, "oh, we were lied to. These people, they came saying, like, they were looking for minerals, and we gave them some minerals, mineral rights there and there. Now they are now saying the land is theirs. They are now chasing away from their… from our lands, they are taking our cattle, they are raping our women, and all trying to convert people into Christianity and all those things." So, they mobilized. They mobilized each other. Another group come from the southern side, from Matabeleland, and the other from the Mashonaland. So there was a country-wide, uprising. It was a war, in fact. Which the Black people lost because, well... One, we didn't have any army, standing army. We didn't have the magazine gun that they had, machine gun that they had, and all those stuff. So, that type of uprising, it's… That's the Chimurenga.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: So there was the first Chimurenga, then the second Chimurenga. The second Chimurenga is this, the one that ushered independence. So when at some point in the 1960s, the black people were fed up again, then they started to take arms. And then there was a 14-year… something, yeah, about 14 years, 16 years, I forgot the numbers, year war that was fought between the white establishment in Zimbabwe and the Black majority, which ushered this independence in 1980. So that's the concept of Chimurenga.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Some people can take it further… That, there was this guy called Murenga, way before, I forgot what did he do, really, in history? But he was a prominent figure. And he was, like, a kind of a fighter, a warrior, and when we say Chimurenga, it's like we are kind of honoring his spirit, the spirit of Murenga and stuff, like, there's a… something like that, I forgot. I can't really speak with, conviction on that, because I'm forgetting the details.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: But there's another narrative that goes that direction in terms of Chimurenga. But, like, what do you call it? Like, generally, generally, Chimurenga is uprising, the two uprisings that happened. The first one, and the… so it's Chimurenga, or Umvukela, in the Ndebele word. So there is the Ndebele version of it, it's the Umvukela. Uprisings.

speaker: Kadallah Burrowes
words: Is it the… is it a… how do I say this? Is it a word that can be used broadly? Or is it only supposed to be used to describe these specific two uprisings?

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: No, like, it can be used, broadly. So… so, when you use it broadly, it's like a revolution. It's like a revolution, so… I said of the two Chimurengas, right? Apparently, they say… There is, there was the third Chimurenga. The third Chimurenga was the one that came with land resettlement, when the Black establishment in Zimbabwe decided to take away land from the whites. So it's… you see, like, there was this revolutionary move, like, period of, like, "okay, now we are turning the land, we are taking the land, so we are in the third Chimurenga."

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: It's kinda, being abused the way people just abused this idea of a third world war. Like, oh, now we are in third world war because now there's AI. Third world war because there's war in Ukraine, Russia is doing this, and they're trying to say, like, if a world is… if the world is being affected at the same time by the acts of this authoritarian rule, whether it's Russia or it's China, or now we are in the Third World War. So it's kind of like the way they use it in Zimbabwe, when they say, third Chimurenga, when we were taking the land away from the whites, now we are taking what is ours, now it's third Chimurenga.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: The fourth Chimurenga that they are talking about now is about them fighting each other, the politicians fighting each other, so there are other people that… Okay, so there, there's some fights within the ruling establishment at the moment. There are people who are getting rich from the establishment. There are people who are saying, "no, this is not what we fought for. So we need to go back to what we fought for to like, feed the masses," like, so there's the word of Gutsaruzhinji. Gutsaruzhinji is, like, feed the masses, everything needs to benefit the masses, not benefit a little, a little few people. So the idea of turning, that idea of, removing the rich, and now going back to the… they are kind of alluding it to the fourth Chimurenga. So, like, that's how loosely they are now, it's now being used at the moment.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: Okay, so… African organizations, they are not... They are used to cooperative organizations. They are used to cooperatives, and they've been doing their own cooperatives for… for years. So, you would approach this cooperative organization, and what they… they're doing what they do best, they knew best. For example, it's a cooperative of African women who are doing vegetable farming. They are farming, they are… they are sharing their profits and everything. They don't have any boss among them, and they say it's theirs, and they own it. They feel the sense of ownership to it. Then, now you come with the idea of DisCO, introducing it to them, which is a new concept most of the time. They would start to… they would start to say, "okay, what is it that is so wrong with what we are doing, that you supp… you… suggested this now, new principles to us? Okay, since it's a new module: how it's going to impact the work that we have been doing all along? If we are now to say, okay, now we are going to cut this work into care work, or cutting this way as productive work, and all the other principles that they just go ahead. If we had to say, okay, now we follow these principles, how is it… how are these principles going to affect our work?" They will ask those important questions. "And, when we are experimenting with this new model, how will be our source of living get affected?"

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: And in trying to answer those questions, they would make a decision, and most of the decision that they will make is that if they can't really say they put their investment, or maybe there's funding, or they… Whatever they are doing in their cooperative, we are setting that aside now to follow this new model, because, one, there is no, anywhere that it has been successful. Second, it's not coming, if it's, when it comes, it's coming to disturb, disrupt the way we were operating, because it was, like, a… like, an operating model. If it disrupts the operating model, we don't know what the impacts on it, like, on our livelihood. Because, mind you, in Africa, most of the times, these cooperatives, will be sustaining lives of people. So, when you're sustaining lives, there's not… there's no, like, there's little room for experimentation. So, they would inquire if there will be, like financial support for them to experiment with this type of model so that they don't take their savings or their funding to direct to this new model that it's trying to prove if it works, yeah.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: What can I call it? I forgot if it's Market Gardening, if it's the real name, the name of it. Like, where we farm, plants that we can go to sell, that we can sell to make a living. So like, those, like, one part of, like, a lot of cooperatives that we had here. So, what we would… they would do, they will raise collectively money to fence the land. It will be fenced. They will collectively raise the money to erect a borehole... Erect a borehole for irrigation, and now they will demarcate land. "This is Kadallah's, this is mine, this is, like, this is your piece of land." Now, what we do is that this one will plant maybe lettuce, the other one will plant some pumpkins, other one will plant another type of vegetables, so that, different type of vegetables, so that we don't, plant one type of vegetable at the… at one time. So, we would rotate, they would rotate. This time, the one who had tomatoes, now they are planting onions. Now, this next time, they are planting this other thing. And whatever they produce, They will take home. If you produce a lot, you buy, go and sell, and you take the profit back home. It wasn't like they would invest in it, but it's just, like, the collective ownership of the land, collective management of the land, collective security, of that land. Then, in terms, during, like, maybe agricultural shows, they will go and show off their produce. Sometimes they get funding, or maybe to put, like, irrigation pipes, or to get fertilizers, they would divide among themselves.

speaker: Brian Tinoota
words: That's, like… but it was done mostly by women. And, like, it seems like cooperatives in Zimbabwe, and in many other African countries, it's, like, mostly done by women. words: Yeah, yeah. So, in terms of structure. Oh, it's a big… It's a big structure. They came together. They create, what they call, like, a regional organization. It's called REPALEAC. It's like, the mother organization of those small organizations in Africa. So then, that regional organization will be a representative in the global alliance. So, there will be a regional organization from Africa, there is a regional organization from Indonesia, which is called AMAN.
